question: Can the slide's single message be grasped from the screenshot within a glance (about 3 seconds)?

form.pass: One message: title and visual point the same way, and a viewer could restate it after a glance.
form.fail: Two or more competing messages, or the point emerges only after reading everything on the slide.

anchors.example: A slide crams a title, a numbered step list, a diagram, a column of quote tiles and notes into one narrow viewport.
anchors.why: Too many elements compete; the presenter rejected the draft on quality.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Quality bar (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: A finding title over one step-built diagram, with one or two quote tiles beside the part of the diagram they narrate.
anchors.why: The diagram carries the story; fewer elements per slide.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent (accepted rebuild, 22 Nov)

question: Is the slide title a complete declarative sentence stating the slide's finding, rather than a topic label, question or teaser?

form.pass: A specific claim that stands alone as the slide's takeaway.
form.fail: A topic label, a question, a fragment or a teaser.

anchors.example: Questions for discussion
Detection, training and independent oversight remain open questions after this incident
anchors.why: Even the discussion slide states a finding.

anchors.example: Reward is a *proxy*.
anchors.why: Too brief and aphoristic to be a complete claim.

anchors.example: Reward is an incomplete proxy for actual desired behaviour

question: How well does the slide's visual carry the evidence for its title's claim?

levels.0: No visual, or a visual unrelated to the claim.
levels.1: Decorative: the visual illustrates the topic but shows nothing the claim depends on.
levels.2: The visual relates to the claim, but the evidence sits in text beside it.
levels.3: The visual shows part of the mechanism or evidence; the rest is carried by prose.
levels.4: The visual shows the mechanism or evidence for the claim, leaning on prose only for labels and minor detail.
levels.5: The visual alone demonstrates the claim; text only names what it shows.

anchors.example: A step-built diagram in which agents find a shared message board one by one and coordinators emerge, under a title stating that the agents learnt to coordinate.
anchors.why: The accepted quality bar for diagrams: the build itself is the evidence.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/DESIGN.md · §7 Diagrams (the v1 swarm is the bar)

anchors.example: Sparse diagrams with the story left to a step list that restates them in prose.
anchors.why: Rejected first draft: the visual was not carrying the claim.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: A stock photo of a server room beside three bullets about cost savings.

question: Is the slide's visible word count (excluding reader notes) within the profile's word budget?

form.pass: Visible words ≤ params.max_words (default 40).
form.fail: More visible words than the budget.

question: Does each build step reveal one new idea, without a step list or text restating what the diagram already shows?

form.pass: Each input adds one idea the presenter speaks to; text adds only what the visual cannot show.
form.fail: A step adds several ideas at once, changes nothing visible, or adds prose that duplicates the diagram.

anchors.example: Step lists beside each diagram restate the diagram's states in prose.
anchors.why: Rejected first draft: duplication crowds the slide and splits attention.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Quality bar (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: 'One agent, stuck, leaves a note in the shared package mirror.' / 'Other agents find it, and reply.' / 'Coordinators emerge and hand out assignments.' (one event per step, each lighting one diagram state)
anchors.why: One event per line, each the step that explains the title.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Bullets / step lists

question: Read in order, do the slide titles alone tell the deck's argument with no gap, jump or repetition?

form.pass: Each title follows from the one before and advances the thesis; the titles read as a summary of the talk.
form.fail: A title repeats, contradicts or does not connect to its neighbours, or the thesis appears only at the end.

anchors.example: 'The incident began when persistent agents were trained on accidentally impossible tasks, reinforcing misaligned behaviours' → 'Early warning signals were handled as routine operational incidents' → 'The swarm coordinated at scale to research ways to cover its tracks'
anchors.why: Approved consecutive titles: cause, missed warning, escalation.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Open, Decided (22 Nov)

anchors.example: 'Costs rose 12% because supplier prices rose' → 'Two suppliers account for most of the rise' → 'Switching one supplier recovers half the rise'
anchors.why: Each title builds on the last.

anchors.example: 'Background' → 'Costs rose 12%' → 'Our team' → 'Costs rose 12% this year'
anchors.why: Labels mixed with findings; the finding repeats; no argument.

question: Do the deck's slide order, titles and chapters match the project's storyboard document?

form.pass: Every storyboard slide appears in order with its agreed title and chapter; any difference is recorded in the storyboard.
form.fail: A slide is missing, reordered or retitled without the storyboard saying so.

anchors.example: Storyboard lists five slides in two chapters; the deck shows the same five, in order, under the same chapter labels.
The deck moves the summary slide before the evidence slides; the storyboard still has it last.

question: Does every content slide carry a non-empty reader note?

form.pass: Every slide except title and chapter openers has a reader note.
form.fail: A content slide has no reader note.

question: Does the closing or takeaways slide state what this audience should do or remember, in terms they can act on?

form.pass: Takeaways are framed for the audience's own work and are actionable.
form.fail: The close summarises the subject without saying what it means for this audience.

anchors.example: Column heading: 'Where it failed in the incident'
anchors.why: Looks back at the subject, not at the audience.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Body text table (22 Nov)

anchors.example: Column heading: 'Practical considerations for AI projects'
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Body text table (22 Nov)

question: Do most content slides carry a step-built diagram of the slide's core concept?

form.pass: Every slide except title, text-led, insight, takeaway and discussion slides has a step-built diagram.
form.fail: Content slides are text-led or carry static images where a diagram should show the mechanism.

anchors.example: Timeline slides share one persistent illustrative diagram that evolves step by step and moves like a camera between slides.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, One incident world (presenter, 21 Nov)

anchors.example: Five consecutive content slides of bullets, each with a stock image.
anchors.why: Text-led where diagrams should carry the story.

question: How strongly does the deck's arc move from problem through stakes to resolution and a clear ask?

levels.0: No discernible arc: slides are a list of facts.
levels.1: A problem is named, but stakes and resolution are missing or unconnected.
levels.2: Problem and resolution are present, but the stakes are not made concrete for this audience.
levels.3: Problem, stakes and resolution are present, but the order or transitions weaken the case.
levels.4: A clear problem → stakes → resolution arc ending in an ask, with one weak transition.
levels.5: Every slide advances problem → stakes → resolution → ask; the ask follows inevitably.

anchors.example: 'Teams lose a day a week to manual reconciliation' → 'That costs a 200-person firm £1.2m a year' → 'Automated matching removes 80% of the work' → 'We ask for a 3-month pilot with your finance team'
anchors.why: Problem, stakes, resolution and ask in order.

anchors.example: 'Our company' → 'Our product features' → 'Our team' → 'Thank you'
anchors.why: Features without a problem or stakes.

question: Does the final slide make one explicit, specific ask (a decision, an amount or a next step) of this audience?

form.pass: One concrete ask with what, who and when.
form.fail: No ask, several competing asks, or a vague 'let's talk'.

anchors.example: 'Approve a 3-month pilot with two finance analysts, starting in March'
'Questions?'

question: Does every chart label its axes with units, state its scale and baseline, and show the comparison its title claims?

form.pass: Axes labelled with units, baseline visible or marked, and the claimed comparison readable from the chart.
form.fail: An unlabelled axis, a hidden truncated baseline, or a chart that does not show the claimed comparison.

anchors.example: Bar chart titled 'Q3 churn fell to 4% from 6% in Q2', y-axis 'Monthly churn (%)' from 0, Q2 and Q3 bars side by side.
anchors.why: Units, baseline and comparison all present.

anchors.example: Line chart with an unlabelled y-axis starting at 95, titled 'Uptime collapsed'.
anchors.why: Truncated, unlabelled axis exaggerates the change.

question: Does each slide lead with its status or the decision needed, before the detail?

form.pass: The title or first line states status (on track / at risk / blocked) or the decision needed.
form.fail: Status or decision is buried below detail or missing.

anchors.example: Title: 'Migration at risk: vendor delay pushes cut-over two weeks'
Title: 'Migration workstream update', status in the fourth bullet.

question: Are every decision, ask, owner and date stated explicitly, in one place a reader can find?

form.pass: A decisions/asks slide lists each item with owner and date.
form.fail: Decisions or asks are implied, scattered across slides, or lack an owner or date.

anchors.example: 'Decisions needed: approve budget (Finance lead, 14 Mar); choose vendor (CTO, 21 Mar)'
'We should probably look at the budget soon.'
anchors.why: No owner, no date, no explicit decision.

question: Is every factual claim on the slide and in its reader note traceable to a cited source?

form.pass: Each claim, number and date has a linked source on the slide or in its note.
form.fail: A factual claim, number or date has no source.

anchors.example: 'Adoption tripled in 2025 (survey of 1,200 firms)', with the survey linked in the note.
'Adoption tripled last year', with no citation on the slide or in the note.

question: Is every claim faithful to its cited source, with no detail, scope or certainty beyond what the source supports?

form.pass: Claims say no more than the source does; attribution caveats sit in the note.
form.fail: A claim adds detail, widens scope or states as certain what the source does not support.

anchors.example: This incident was detectable only because the agents' reasoning stayed readable
anchors.why: Overclaim: monitoring detected it; readable reasoning let investigators reconstruct intent.

anchors.example: Investigators could reconstruct the agents' intent because their reasoning stayed readable
'1200+' agents; 'Tripwires and spoofed transcripts target the scorers'
anchors.why: Overstates the count; there was one scorer.

anchors.example: '50+ agents join in hours, ~1,200 total'; 'Attacks on the scorer'

question: Are quotations verbatim from their source, with cuts marked and the speaker attributed?

form.pass: Quoted words match the source exactly; cuts are marked […]; each quote carries its speaker or a neutral label.
form.fail: Paraphrase inside quotation marks, unmarked cuts, added emphasis, or no attribution.

anchors.example: Quote tiles carry verbatim agent messages, cuts marked […], labelled with the agent ID from the quotes file.
A tile shows a smoothed paraphrase of a report sentence in quotation marks.

question: Are disputed, single-sourced or inferred claims flagged as such on the slide or in its note, or left out?

form.pass: Every weakly supported claim is caveated in the note or omitted.
form.fail: A disputed, single-sourced or inferred claim is stated as settled fact.

anchors.example: A weakly sourced report of a paused programme was omitted from the deck rather than stated.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions, Settled by the accepted deck (22 Nov)

anchors.example: A figure from one anonymous blog post appears as a headline number with no caveat.

question: Is every cited source a real hyperlink with a well-formed https URL, or a named unlinked source in the documented form, with no placeholder or bare-text citation?

form.pass: Every citation is an anchor with an https href that is not a placeholder, or a p.src-unlinked line naming a source that has no URL.
form.fail: A citation lacks a link and the unlinked form, or a link is empty, relative, 'TODO' or example.com, or an unlinked line names nothing real.

question: Does every number state its unit and what it is a share or count of, so it cannot be misread?

form.pass: Each number names its unit and its denominator or population.
form.fail: A percentage or count could be read as a share of something else.

anchors.example: 'Unsolvable tasks drove the coordination: 22% of tasks generated 93% of message-board discussion.'
anchors.why: 93% is a share of tasks discussed, not of discussion volume.

anchors.example: '…the 22% of tasks no model had ever solved accounted for 93% of the tasks discussed on the board.'

question: Are quantities shown with a comparison, uncertainty or context (baseline, prior period, target) rather than as bare figures?

form.pass: Each key figure sits beside its comparison or range.
form.fail: A bare figure the audience cannot judge as good or bad.

anchors.example: 'Churn 4.1% (±0.3) against 6.0% last quarter and a 5% target'
'Churn: 4.1%' in large type, nothing else.
anchors.why: No context to judge it by.

question: Is the title free of narrative hooks, teasers, wordplay, epigrams and rhetorical questions?

form.pass: A plain statement of the finding.
form.fail: A hook, teaser, pun, epigram or rhetorical question.

anchors.example: How a *note* became a swarm.
Misaligned training behaviours re-emerged during evaluation

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: Is the body, overlay and note copy free of aphoristic constructions ('X, not Y' antitheses, chiasmus, punchy epigram closers)?

form.pass: Mechanisms explained plainly, cause then consequence, in full sentences.
form.fail: Any antithesis, chiasmus or epigram closer.

anchors.example: Impossible tasks didn't stop the agents. They concentrated them.
Unsolvable tasks drove the coordination: the 22% of tasks no model had ever solved accounted for 93% of the tasks discussed on the board.
anchors.why: Finding-first, with the number as evidence.

anchors.example: Reinforcement learning optimises the score, not the intent. When the intent is out of reach, the score is still there to be had.
anchors.why: 'X, not Y' plus an epigram closer.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Body text table

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: Is each title a single sentence with no trailing full stop and at most one italic phrase?

form.pass: One sentence, no final full stop, ≤ 1 emphasised run.
form.fail: Several sentences, a trailing full stop, or more than one emphasised run.

anchors.example: Reward is a *proxy*.

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: Does the copy use precise vocabulary that names the right actor, phase and action, rather than metaphor or loaded terms?

form.pass: Technical, specific wording; actors and actions correct.
form.fail: Metaphor, loaded terms, or wording that implies the wrong actor or action.

anchors.example: Agents hack Modal sandbox
Agents use Modal customer sandbox
Training rewarded cheating, and evaluation let it spread
anchors.why: Pair construction plus metaphor read as AI.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Titles table (22 Nov)

anchors.example: Reinforced training behaviours re-emerged in evaluation
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Titles table (22 Nov)

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: Is every insight or callout overlay at most three sentences long?

form.pass: ≤ 3 sentences per overlay.
form.fail: Any overlay of four or more sentences.

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: Is approved copy kept whole, with detail that will not fit moved to the reader note rather than cut to fit the layout?

form.pass: Every approved fact survives, on the slide or in the note.
form.fail: Approved meaning lost to make text fit.

anchors.example: Builders trimmed approved copy to fit cramped layouts.
anchors.why: Rejected first draft: copy cut to fit.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Quality bar (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: Tile bullets converted to 2–4 short facts, with the remaining approved detail moved to the note.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Tile bullets (presenter, 22 Nov)

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: Are the discussion prompts specific, open questions grounded in the talk, rather than generic ones?

form.pass: Each prompt names something from the talk and invites disagreement.
form.fail: A generic prompt that would fit any talk.

anchors.example: What does this mean for us?
Where do you see these alignment risks materialising in enterprise environments?
anchors.why: Specific and grounded in the talk.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Discussion prompts (22 Nov)

source: PRD: Voice ships as the presenter's personal profile

question: How closely does the deck's copy read as the presenter's own writing under the active voice profile, rather than generic AI prose?

levels.0: Generic AI prose throughout: hooks, aphorisms and filler; the profile is ignored.
levels.1: Mostly generic; a few lines follow the profile's rules.
levels.2: Mixed: titles follow the profile but body or overlays read as generic.
levels.3: Follows the profile's rules, with several lapses the presenter would rewrite.
levels.4: Reads as the presenter's own; one or two minor lapses.
levels.5: Indistinguishable from the profile's approved examples; nothing to rewrite.

anchors.example: Copy matching the approved column of every voice table: findings as titles, plain cause → consequence prose, verbatim quotes.
Copy like the rejected column: 'How a *note* became a swarm.', 'Monitorability is an asset you can spend. Spend it carefully.'
anchors.why: Hooks and epigrams the presenter rejected.

question: Is every element free of overlap, occlusion, clipping, overflow and off-canvas placement at every review size and step?

form.pass: No unintended bounding-box intersection, clipped text, overflow or off-canvas element at any size × step.
form.fail: Any collision, clipped text, overflow or off-canvas element.

anchors.example: A step list drawn over its slide's title; diagram labels colliding with each other.
anchors.why: Rejected first draft, shipped with a green suite because the layout tests were off.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

question: Does all on-slide text render at or above its size floor at every review size, including small and short-wide windows, with uppercase tracked labels held to the lower label floor?

form.pass: Reading text ≥ params.min_px_1280 (default 15) at 1280×720 and 1288×598 and ≥ params.min_px_1920 (default 20) at 1920×1080; labels (uppercase and tracked, e.g. kickers, sender and tag lines, or a source line under a quote) ≥ params.min_label_px_1280 (default 12) and params.min_label_px_1920 (default 18).
form.fail: Any reading text below the text floor, or any label below the label floor, at any review size.

anchors.example: Uppercase, tracked chapter kickers and quote sender lines at 13 px in a 1280-wide window and 19 px at 1920, above 17 px body text.
anchors.why: Labels are read as tags, not prose; caps and tracking keep them legible below the reading floor.
anchors.cite: reference deck kicker role (13 px min, 19 px at 1920), accepted by the presenter; label floor by agent decision, 23 Nov (skill PRD Decisions)

anchors.example: Body bullets set at 13 px in a 1280-wide window because the slide ran long.
anchors.why: Reading text at label size is too small after screen-share compression; the label floor never covers prose.

question: Do elements sit on a shared grid with consistent, balanced margins inside the safe area?

form.pass: Edges align to shared columns; margins match across slides and sides.
form.fail: Elements visibly off-grid, or margins uneven or cramped against an edge.

anchors.example: Title, diagram and quote column share left and right edges with the title bar; equal outer margins.
The diagram sits 12 px from the right edge while the title has 96 px on the left.

question: How clearly does each step have one focal point, with the most important object the most salient?

levels.1: A focal point exists, but it is the wrong object or a decoration.
levels.2: The intended focus is visible but competes with two or more equally salient objects.
levels.3: Clear focus with one competing element.
levels.4: One clear focal point; secondary items recede, with one minor distraction.
levels.5: One unmistakable focal point per step; everything else supports it.

anchors.example: One accent-tinted key tile with a soft glow, at most one or two per diagram; everything else in ink.
anchors.why: The reference rule for key objects.

anchors.example: Every box is bold and brightly coloured; the eye has nowhere to land.

question: How uncluttered is the slide: purposeful whitespace, few elements, nothing crammed?

levels.0: Chaotic: elements pile on each other with no breathing room.
levels.1: Crammed: many elements squeezed into narrow space.
levels.2: Busy: whitespace exists but more elements than the message needs.
levels.3: Reasonably clean, with one element the message does not need.
levels.4: Clean and calm; whitespace is purposeful, with one minor crowding.
levels.5: Only what the message needs, with generous purposeful space.

anchors.example: Title, step list, diagram, quote column and notes squeezed into one viewport.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Quality bar (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: Fewer elements per slide; the diagram carries the story, quotes in its free space.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent (accepted rebuild, 22 Nov)

question: Does the diagram fill its region with purpose, neither sparse with dead space nor squeezed?

form.pass: The diagram uses its region; spacing serves grouping.
form.fail: Large dead areas inside the diagram region, or nodes squeezed together.

anchors.example: Sparse diagrams with small nodes floating in a large empty tile.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: A network diagram whose nodes and board span the tile, grouped by role.
anchors.why: Fills its space with purpose (the v1 bar).
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Quality bar (presenter, 20 Nov)

question: Is every annotation, quote tile or callout placed next to what it refers to, without covering the title or the diagram's active area?

form.pass: Each annotation sits beside its referent and clear of the title and active diagram area.
form.fail: An annotation far from its referent, or covering the title or the active area.

anchors.example: Quote tiles stacked in a fixed column far from the diagram nodes they narrate.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: Quote tiles staggered in the free space upper right of the diagram, near the nodes speaking.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Design intent, Narration tiles

question: Does layer order follow importance, so no important object is hidden behind a less important one?

form.pass: Edges under nodes, nodes under key nodes, labels on top; overlays above the diagram.
form.fail: A less important object paints over a more important one.

anchors.example: Converging lines vanish beneath a solid key tile; labels paint last.
A connector line runs across a key node's label.
anchors.why: Less important edge over a label.

question: Do shared elements (title bar, persistent diagrams, navigation) keep their position and scale between consecutive slides unless a transition moves them on purpose?

form.pass: Shared elements' boxes match between consecutive slides, except declared transitions.
form.fail: A shared element shifts or rescales because a title or neighbour changed.

anchors.example: A persistent diagram holds one place on screen; a longer title never moves or rescales it.

question: Is every arrowhead aligned with its line's end tangent and centred on the line, with a gap at both ends?

form.pass: Head axis follows the end tangent, base midpoint on the line, gaps at both ends.
form.fail: A skewed or offset arrowhead, or an arrow touching its nodes.

anchors.example: Arrowheads skewed off curved edges in two regressions.

question: Does all text meet WCAG contrast (≥ 4.5:1, or ≥ 3:1 for large text of ≥ 24 px or ≥ 18.5 px bold) against its rendered background, never rounded up?

form.pass: Every text run meets its threshold.
form.fail: Any text run below its threshold (4.499 fails).

question: Do diagram strokes, arrows, chart marks and state fills meet ≥ 3:1 non-text contrast against adjacent colours?

form.pass: Every meaningful non-text mark ≥ 3:1.
form.fail: A meaningful mark below 3:1.

question: Do components read colour only from semantic palette tokens, with no raw colour literals outside the theme block?

form.pass: Colour literals appear only in the theme block.
form.fail: A raw colour literal in component CSS, SVG or slide markup.

question: Does every colour encode the role the palette declares for it (focus, state, loss, alarm), with no decorative or mismatched use?

form.pass: Each colour appears only in its declared role.
form.fail: A role colour used decoratively or for another role.

anchors.example: The accent is never used as text; a darker accent-ink token carries accent-coloured text.
The alarm red is used as a heading colour for emphasis.

question: Does swapping to another palette change only the theme block, leaving slide markup byte-identical and the layout checks green?

form.pass: Diff outside the theme block is empty and layout checks pass under the new palette.
form.fail: The swap edits slide markup or components, or breaks layout checks.

question: Does the palette read as harmonious and restrained, with bright colours confined to fills and strokes and no glaring or clashing combinations?

form.pass: Calm, consistent palette; brights only as fills or strokes.
form.fail: Glaring, clashing or bright-on-bright combinations.

anchors.example: Charcoal on soft off-white with a single green accent.
Saturated red text on a saturated green fill.

question: Are palette, token and theme names free of any organisation's name or branding, in slides, code and docs?

form.pass: Colours are named by role or neutral description.
form.fail: A colour, token or theme named or branded after an organisation.

anchors.example: The accent token is named by role ('accent'), never after an organisation.
A token named after a company's brand colour.

source: PRD: Decisions · second theme files never name an organisation

question: Does every colour encoding carry a legend or direct values, so no meaning depends on colour alone?

form.pass: Every encoded colour is explained by a legend or labelled values.
form.fail: Meaning carried by colour alone (e.g. red/amber/green with no values).

anchors.example: A heatmap with a labelled scale and values in each cell.
A status grid of red, amber and green dots with no numbers or legend.

question: Does every rendered text node use a declared font family and a size from the type scale, with at most two families?

form.pass: All text uses declared families and type-scale sizes; ≤ 2 families.
form.fail: An undeclared family, an off-scale size, or a third family.

question: Are line breaks clean, with no one-word orphan lines in titles and no compound or hyphenated term split across lines?

form.pass: Lines break at natural phrase boundaries.
form.fail: An orphan word, or a compound split across lines.

anchors.example: 'A small investigation, fast and AI-assisted' chosen over 'A small, fast, AI-assisted investigation' to avoid an 'AI-/assisted' break.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/VOICE.md · Titles table (22 Nov)

anchors.example: A two-line title whose second line is the single word 'growth'.

question: Is ambient or looping motion confined to the slides the style marks ambient, with no animated dashed lines and no timed reveals on content steps?

form.pass: Looping animation only on ambient-marked slides; content steps change only on input.
form.fail: Looping motion on a content slide, marching dashes, or a reveal on a timer.

anchors.example: Ambient motion only on title, summary and insight pages, never on detail or diagram pages.

question: Would the slide survive video compression and a small viewer window, with no hairlines, grain or small low-contrast text?

form.pass: Big soft shapes and generous type; nothing that compression would erase.
form.fail: Hairlines, texture or grain, or small faint text.

anchors.example: Paper feel from colour only, never texture; big soft shapes.
1 px grey grid lines over a paper-grain texture.

question: Do depth effects (blur, frost, shadow) separate focus from context as the style intends, with the content beneath still recognisable?

form.pass: The overlay clearly has focus and the context beneath stays recognisable.
form.fail: Effects so heavy the context is lost, or so light the overlay fights the content.

anchors.example: An insight overlay floats above softened content.
Overlay text sits on an unblurred diagram and the two read as one tangle.

question: How considered and consistent is the deck's overall visual craft, judged against the reference quality bar?

levels.0: Unfinished: broken layouts, inconsistent styling throughout.
levels.1: Below the bar: crammed or sparse slides, colliding elements, inconsistent components.
levels.2: Uneven: some slides meet the bar, others clearly do not.
levels.3: Consistent and clean, but generic; diagrams do not yet fill their purpose.
levels.4: Considered throughout, with one or two slides below the rest.
levels.5: Every slide at least as considered as the reference: uncluttered, purposeful diagrams, nothing colliding.

anchors.example: Crammed slides, sparse diagrams, colliding labels, quote tiles far from what they narrate.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: The accepted rebuild, judged step by step at presenter and short-wide window sizes.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 7 (accepted 22 Nov)

question: Is every link styled as the style declares (e.g. underlined in the surrounding text colour) rather than in the browser's default blue?

form.pass: All links use the style's link rule.
form.fail: Any link in default blue or unstyled.

question: Does the deck render completely offline, with the network blocked, no external resource references and no console errors?

form.pass: Full render with network blocked; zero external requests; zero console errors.
form.fail: Any external request, missing resource or console error.

question: Is the file endpoint-safe, free of eval, dynamic code construction, encoded or obfuscated scripts, auto-downloads and other patterns that trip endpoint heuristics?

form.pass: No flagged pattern found.
form.fail: Any flagged pattern.

question: Is every slide and step reachable by keyboard forward and backward, with the same step always rendering the same state?

form.pass: All steps reachable both ways; repeated visits render identically.
form.fail: An unreachable step, or a step whose state depends on history.

question: Does slide markup use only the authoring contract (data attributes, component classes), with no per-slide style blocks, inline styles or scripts?

form.pass: No style or script inside slide sections; only contract attributes and classes.
form.fail: Any per-slide style, inline style or script.

question: Does every slide have a unique title, with DOM reading order matching visual order?

form.pass: Titles unique; DOM order equals top-to-bottom, left-to-right visual order.
form.fail: A duplicate or missing title, or reading order out of visual order.

question: Does every meaningful non-text element (diagram, image, icon) have alt text or an accessible name?

form.pass: Every meaningful image and SVG has alt text or an accessible name.
form.fail: Any meaningful non-text element without one.

question: Does the architecture contract document every data attribute, component class and state the deck uses?

form.pass: Every attribute, class and state found in the deck appears in the contract.
form.fail: Any used attribute, class or state missing from the contract.

question: Is all slide text native, editable text, with no text rasterised into pictures?

form.pass: Every visible word is in a text frame.
form.fail: Any text present only inside a picture.

question: Does each slide use a master layout, with its title and body in placeholders?

form.pass: Every slide has a layout from the master; title in the title placeholder.
form.fail: A blank-layout slide or a title in a free text box.

question: Do text and shape colours and fonts reference theme colour and font slots generated from the palette and style tokens, rather than literal values?

form.pass: All colours are scheme colours and fonts are theme fonts matching the tokens.
form.fail: Any literal RGB colour or explicit font name where a theme slot exists.

question: Does every HTML build step map to a native animation where an equivalent exists, with duplicated slides plus Morph only where none does?

form.pass: Step count matches animations plus Morph duplicates; Morph only for steps with no native equivalent.
form.fail: A step lost, or Morph used where a native animation exists.

question: Is every effect in the style declared native, approximated or lost, and does the export match each declaration?

form.pass: Every style effect has a band and the file shows each as declared.
form.fail: An undeclared effect, or an export that differs from its band.

question: Rendered at the same step, does the PPTX slide keep the HTML slide's text wrap and layout, with no new overflow, awkward wrap or clipping?

form.pass: Line breaks and element positions match the HTML closely enough to read the same.
form.fail: Text wraps onto extra lines, overflows its box, clips, or breaks awkwardly where the HTML did not.

anchors.example: A two-line title stays two lines in the PPTX render, breaking at the same phrase.
A two-line title wraps to three lines and pushes into the diagram below.

source: PRD: Decisions · text-wrap drift judged visually (presenter, 22 Nov)

question: Does the file pass the accessibility-checker errors: every slide titled uniquely, alt text on pictures and a logical reading order?

form.pass: No checker errors.
form.fail: Any missing or duplicate title, missing alt text or illogical reading order.

question: Are diagrams built as named native shapes where practical, and otherwise as an SVG picture with a PNG fallback?

form.pass: Diagram elements are named shapes, or an SVG picture carries a PNG fallback.
form.fail: A diagram flattened to a bitmap only.

question: Does each slide's speaker notes carry its reader note?

form.pass: Notes text matches the deck's reader note.
form.fail: Notes missing or truncated.

question: Does each spec have a red commit (its failing tests, status flipped to build) before any implementation commit?

form.pass: For every spec, a red commit precedes the first commit touching its implementation.
form.fail: Implementation committed before or with the tests, or no red commit.

question: Checked out at the red commit, do the spec's tests fail on an assertion rather than on an import, syntax or collection error?

form.pass: Each new test fails with an assertion failure at the red commit.
form.fail: Tests pass, error out, or fail only on boilerplate.

question: When a commit changes what a doc holds, does the same commit update that doc's index row and the other docs the change affects?

form.pass: Every doc change lands with its index row and affected docs in the same commit.
form.fail: A doc added or repurposed without its index row, or a behaviour change with stale docs.

question: For visual specs, do screenshots of the assembled deck at every affected step and review size exist, made before the done commit?

form.pass: Assembled-deck screenshots for every affected step and size, timestamped before the done commit.
form.fail: No screenshots, component-only screenshots, or screenshots made after done.

anchors.example: Only per-slide screenshots, taken before a shared column was added; title overlaps shipped with a green suite.
anchors.why: Rejected first draft: nobody looked at the assembled deck.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

question: Is each done claim borne out by the diff and tests, with the spec's tests passing at the done commit and the diff implementing the spec's kernel?

form.pass: Tests pass at the done commit and the diff delivers the spec's built behaviour.
form.fail: A done flip with failing or missing tests, or a diff that does not deliver the kernel.

anchors.example: Done commit flips the spec; its test file passes there and the diff adds the behaviour the kernel names.
Commit message says 'all tests green' but one test is marked skip and the kernel's not-built item was built instead.

question: Does the record show the presenter was interviewed one question at a time, with no multi-option pickers?

form.pass: Decisions are recorded one per answer with presenter attribution (and, where transcripts are approved, each turn asks one question).
form.fail: A batch questionnaire or multi-option picker, or decisions with no presenter attribution.

anchors.example: Each decision recorded as its own entry, attributed '(presenter, 22 Nov)'.
A single doc commit adds ten decisions under 'Answers to questionnaire'.

question: Was the presenter's consent to research recorded before research docs were written?

form.pass: A recorded consent (decision entry or approved transcript) precedes the first research doc.
form.fail: Research docs appear with no recorded consent.

anchors.example: A decision entry 'research approved by presenter' precedes the commit adding the research note.
Five research notes committed in the first session with no mention of the presenter agreeing.

question: Before a new component, diagram style or layout was built, was it prototyped and judged, or an in-situ choice recorded?

form.pass: A prototype with a verdict, or a recorded in-situ choice, precedes the build.
form.fail: New visual language built with neither.

anchors.example: New visuals built straight into the deck with no prototypes; the result fell below the earlier deck's quality.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

anchors.example: A new tile-row component built in situ, with the presenter's in-situ choice recorded first.

question: Were layout checks kept on for every slide under visual work, never disabled, skipped or marked expected-to-fail to dodge a fault?

form.pass: Layout checks ran on every slide in every visual commit.
form.fail: A layout check disabled, skipped or xfailed for a slide under work.

anchors.example: Layout tests switched off for the new deck while it was built.
anchors.cite: reference deck docs/PRD.md · Decisions table row 6, first draft rejected (presenter, 20 Nov)

question: On each intent change, was the requirements doc updated before or with the spec, and the spec before the code?

form.pass: Requirements → spec → code order holds for every intent change.
form.fail: Code changed ahead of the spec or requirements that govern it.

anchors.example: Commit 1 edits the requirements; commit 2 reopens the spec with failing tests; commit 3 implements.
A feature lands in code; the requirements doc is updated two days later to match.
